Three weeks before the semester exams, Wasim's desk in the paying-guest room was covered in charger cables and unopened notes. "Relax," he told his classmate Disha on a call. "I work better under pressure. Last-minute is my style."
He said it every evening, between long cricket videos and trips to the chai stall. It sounded confident. Inside, it was different. Every time he opened the thermodynamics book, he remembered the forty-one he had got in the mid-term, and his chest tightened. Closing the book felt like relief.
On the Sunday before exams he finally opened it at midnight and couldn't follow the first chapter. "Pressure" felt a lot like panic. He messaged Disha: "Can we study together tomorrow? Honestly, I think I've been scared of this subject."

qa.q: What mark did Wasim get in the mid-term?
qa.a: Wasim got forty-one in the mid-term.

qa.q: What was Wasim really afraid of when he kept closing the book?
qa.a: He was afraid of failing again; remembering the forty-one tightened his chest, and closing the book brought relief.

qa.q: What choice on the Sunday before exams was a good turning point?
qa.a: Wasim admitted to Disha that he had been scared and asked to study together, replacing the story with a real plan.

qa.q: How might Disha see "I work better under pressure" after the midnight message?
qa.a: Disha might have believed it at first, but the honest message shows the confidence was covering fear.

grounding: A student skips weeks of study and calls it working better under pressure, a story that shields him from his fear of failing.

"You've been on that sofa since lunch," Rekha said. "Aren't your exams in a month?"
"I'm resting my brain, Didi. I study best in the last two weeks. Always have."
"Always? Last year you cried the whole night before accounts."
"That was different."
"How?"
Disha pulled a cushion over her face. "Because that time I actually studied and still did badly, okay?"
Rekha sat down beside her. "So if you don't study and it goes badly..."
"...then it's because I didn't study. Not because I'm stupid." Disha went quiet. "That sounds bad when I say it out loud."
"It sounds scared," Rekha said. "One hour together after dinner? Just one."
"Fine. One hour."

qa.q: What happened the night before accounts last year?
qa.a: Disha cried the whole night before accounts.

qa.q: What does "then it's because I didn't study" reveal about Disha's fear?
qa.a: It reveals that Disha is afraid of trying hard and still failing, so not studying protects the belief of not being stupid.

qa.q: What small step does Rekha suggest, and why might it work?
qa.a: Rekha suggests one hour together after dinner, which is small enough to start without facing the whole fear at once.

qa.q: How does Rekha see Disha's "resting my brain"?
qa.a: Rekha sees through it and recognises fear rather than laziness, which is why the reply is gentle: "It sounds scared."

grounding: A student tells Rekha Didi about studying best at the last minute, and the talk uncovers the fear of failing that the story protects.

passage:
In the small town of Ambala Cantt, the carrom board at Tarun's cycle-repair shop saw more of Ujjwal in exam month than his books did.
"Prep leave is for relaxing, bhai," Ujjwal said, flicking the striker. "I work better under pressure. Last week before exams, I become a machine."
Tarun, who had failed the same second-year paper once, lined up his shot. "Last year you said the same. You got a backlog in maths."
"That was different. Bad paper."
"And the year before?"
Ujjwal missed the red queen. He laughed too loudly. "Why are you so serious?"
That night, when the house was quiet, he took out the maths book and opened it at the first chapter. His chest went tight. What if he started early, worked hard, and still failed? Then there'd be no excuse left.
He closed the book and picked up his phone.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal get in maths last year?
qa.a: He got a backlog in maths.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's chest go tight when he opened the maths book?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt afraid that if he studied early and still failed, he would have no excuse left, so the "pressure" story protected him.

qa.q: What small step could help Ujjwal face the fear?
qa.a: He could study just one chapter a day with Tarun or a teacher, and admit that fear of failing, not pressure, is what stops him.

qa.q: How does Tarun see Ujjwal's claim about pressure?
qa.a: Tarun doubts it, because he remembers the backlog, and he quietly pushes Ujjwal to see the pattern.

grounding: It shows a student rationalising weeks of avoiding study as working better under pressure, while the real driver is fear of failing.

passage:
In the shared kitchen of their Dublin flat, Nadia was making her third tea of the evening. Her thesis draft, due in nine days, had one paragraph.
"You okay?" asked Liam, her flatmate, stirring pasta.
"Totally. I'm one of those people who works better with a deadline. Adrenaline, you know?"
Liam nodded slowly. "Like second year? The stats exam?"
Nadia laughed. "That was a one-off."
She had failed that exam. She had resat it in August, alone, while everyone else was on holiday.
Back in her room she opened the draft. The cursor blinked. Every sentence she typed looked stupid. What if she really tried, and her supervisor still said it was weak? At least if she wrote it in three nights, she could say she hadn't had time.
She closed the laptop and went back to the kitchen. "Liam, can I tell you something? I think I'm scared."

qa.q: How many days until the thesis draft is due?
qa.a: It is due in nine days.

qa.q: What was Nadia worried about when she stared at the blinking cursor?
qa.a: Nadia was afraid that trying her hardest and still being called weak would hurt more than failing with the excuse of no time.

qa.q: What choice at the end could help Nadia?
qa.a: Telling Liam she is scared is a good first step; she could also book a meeting with her supervisor and write a little each day.

qa.q: How does Liam seem to see the "adrenaline" story?
qa.a: Liam seems doubtful and gently concerned, since he remembers the stats exam she failed.

grounding: It shows a student telling herself she works best under pressure while avoiding her thesis, until she admits the fear of failing underneath.

The girls' hostel study room was full the week before semester exams, but Nirmala's corner had the same closed notes it had held since September.
"Coming to the library?" her roommate Payal asked.
"No, I'll do it all in the last three days. I'm one of those people. My brain wakes up under pressure."
"You said that before the mid-sems," Payal said gently. "Then you cried the whole night before the chemistry paper."
Nirmala shrugged, but her fingers went white around her pen.
Later, when Payal left, the hostel warden came by, checking rooms. "Everything all right, beta? You look worried."
Nirmala almost said "fine." Instead she said, "If I start now and still fail, then I really am stupid."
The warden pulled up a chair. "Let's look at one chapter together. Just one. Then you can go see the student counsellor tomorrow."

qa.q: When did Nirmala say she would do all her studying?
qa.a: In the last three days.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's grip on her pen suggest?
qa.a: Her white fingers suggest Nirmala feels frightened and tense, and that the "pressure" story hides a fear of failing.

qa.q: How did the warden support Nirmala?
qa.a: The warden sat down, suggested one chapter together, and pointed her toward the student counsellor the next day.

qa.q: How does Payal see Nirmala's plan?
qa.a: Payal is worried for her, remembering the night Nirmala cried before the chemistry paper.

grounding: It shows a student rationalising skipped study as working better under pressure, which covers a fear of failing.

Hi Maria,
Exams start in nine days and I haven't opened the organic chemistry notes since August. Don't panic on my behalf! You know me, I work better under pressure. Last year I did the whole thermodynamics unit in two nights and passed.
I've been busy anyway: the dance club, the new series everyone's watching, reorganising my room (twice). The room looks great, honestly.
The funny thing is, every time I sit down with the notes, my chest goes tight and I suddenly need to check my phone. Probably just tired.
Actually, if I'm totally honest, which is easier in an email, last year's "pass" was by three marks. And I cried in the bathroom before the exam. So maybe "better under pressure" isn't the whole truth. Maybe I just don't want to find out I can't do it.
Call me this weekend? I might need a study buddy.
Vidya

qa.q: When do Vidya's exams start?
qa.a: Exams start in nine days.

qa.q: What does Vidya's tight chest when opening the notes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vidya is anxious and afraid of failing, which the 'better under pressure' story was covering up.

qa.q: What small step is Vidya taking by the end of the email?
qa.a: Admitting the real reason and asking Maria to be a study buddy this weekend, instead of waiting for the last two nights.

qa.q: How might Maria read this email?
qa.a: Maria might feel worried by the three-mark pass and the crying, and glad Vidya is finally asking for help.

grounding: Shows a student claiming to work better under pressure to avoid the real reason for not studying, a fear of failing.
